before: An interpolated string begins with $. Expressions inside braces are evaluated and inserted into the text, as in $"Score: {score}".

A string value is immutable. Methods such as ToUpperInvariant return another string; they do not rewrite the original variable’s value unless you assign that result.

ToUpperInvariant() takes no arguments and returns an uppercased string using invariant culture: fixed casing rules rather than the user’s current language settings. The receiver remains unchanged; a distinct new string object is not promised.

Length counts UTF-16 code units. An index in brackets starts at zero; text[0] reads the first code unit as a char. Some displayed characters use more than one code unit, so Length is not always a count of human-visible symbols.
Calling a method and ignoring its result leaves the original text unchanged. Store the returned value if you need it later.
Expected behavior from this example: stars / STARS. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Display both the original and transformed text. Change the input and show that ignoring ToUpperInvariant’s returned value does not change the original variable. You may trace it on paper if no C# toolchain is installed; reading completion does not certify a run.
after: A string is a value that holds text. Here, topic holds the word stars.
ToUpperInvariant() returns text with uppercase letters. Invariant means it uses fixed letter rules, rather than the computer's chosen language.
A string cannot be changed in place. The method returns a result, which we save in loud. The value in topic stays the same.
A message that starts with $ can include values inside braces. The braces insert the value; they do not appear in the message.
The program prints stars / STARS. The slash is ordinary text between the two values.
Calling the method alone does not replace topic. We keep the returned value in loud so we can display both versions.
